title: The Lost Land That Once Connected Britain to Europe

beats.text: 20,000 years ago, you could walk from Britain to Europe.
beats.say: Twenty thousand years ago, you could walk from Britain to Europe.

beats.text: No boat. No bridge. Just land.

scene.title: DOGGERLAND
scene.subtitle: THE LOST LAND OF THE NORTH SEA

beats.text: In the Ice Age, the sea was about 120 metres lower.
beats.say: In the Ice Age, the sea was about a hundred and twenty metres lower.

beats.text: Where the North Sea is today, there were plains, rivers and marshes.
People lived here. Stone Age hunter-gatherers fished and hunted across it.
Then the ice melted, and the sea crept back in.
By around 6500 BC, Britain was an island.
beats.say: By around sixty-five hundred B.C., Britain was an island.

beats.text: About 8,200 years ago, an undersea landslide off Norway sent a tsunami into the North Sea.
beats.say: About eight thousand two hundred years ago, an undersea landslide off Norway sent a tsunami into the North Sea.

beats.text: In time, even the last islands slipped beneath the waves.
In 1931, a trawler dragged up a lump of peat from the seabed. Inside was a barbed antler point, left by people who lived there.
A lost world, still beneath the North Sea. Follow ORDELVA for more.

facts.claim: Doggerland connected Britain to continental Europe when sea levels were low (during and after the last Ice Age).
sources: Gaffney, Fitch & Smith (2009) Europe's Lost World: The Rediscovery of Doggerland

facts.claim: At the Last Glacial Maximum (~20,000 years ago) sea level was about 120 m lower than today.
The name Doggerland was coined by archaeologist Bryony Coles in the 1990s (after the Dogger Bank).
The Early Holocene landscape included plains, rivers and marshes (seismic mapping, Birmingham team 2003-2007).
Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age) hunter-gatherers lived there; it was a rich hunting, fowling and fishing ground.
Between about 10,000 and 7,000 years ago rising seas flooded Doggerland; Britain was cut off from the continent by around 6500 BC.
The Storegga Slide off Norway, c. 8,200 years ago (c. 6200 BC), caused a tsunami that reached North Sea coasts.
Remaining low islands (e.g. Dogger Bank, an island until at least c. 5000 BC) were eventually submerged.
In 1931 the trawler Colinda hauled up a lump of peat near the Leman and Ower banks containing a barbed antler point (~220 mm).

youtube.description:
20,000 years ago you could walk from Britain to mainland Europe. This is Doggerland: the drowned land beneath the North Sea.

Maps are simplified reconstructions from modern seabed depth (NOAA ETOPO). Landscape and artefact scenes are illustrations.
